cases.title: The DMZ handoff
cases.intro: A 100G member link is down between spine-gw1 and dmz-gw2. Compare the original command captures and their follow-up observations.
cases.method: Compare status at both ends, follow spine Tx toward DMZ Rx, then correlate Local/Remote Fault and repeated MAC histories. Use the supplied diagnosis to choose a targeted replacement and verify its effect. Positive local Tx DOM does not prove delivery to the peer.
cases.limits: Timezone was not supplied. Only MAC outputs carry absolute capture timestamps. Transceiver Last Update values are telemetry ages. Counter reset history and numerical post-repair measurements were not supplied. Spine optic replacement and link recovery were confirmed by the operator. Port-channel IDs are local context, not a diagnosed LACP fault.
cases.collectionNote: MAC snapshots span 41 seconds on spine and 39 seconds on DMZ across midnight. The repeated optics/errors have unspecified capture times; status has one capture per endpoint.

questions.prompt: Which optic has failed, and what should you replace?

options.text: The dmz-gw2 Et6/21/1 optic has failed; replace it because its Rx power is -30.00 dBm.
options.feedback: The low DMZ receive reading points back toward the spine transmitter. Read it together with Remote Fault True on the spine.

options.text: The spine-gw1 Et6/2/1 optic has failed; replace it. Spine Remote Fault True is backed up by -30.00 dBm Rx on dmz-gw2.
options.feedback: Correct. The combined evidence points to the spine optic as the failed component to replace in this case.

options.text: Neither optic needs replacing because both ports show zero error counters.
options.feedback: Zero error counters do not explain away the down link, Remote Fault or missing receive signal.

questions.explanation: Spine Remote Fault True reports that the peer is having trouble receiving its signal. DMZ Local Fault True and -30.00 dBm on all four DMZ receive channels back this up. In this case, diagnose a failed spine-gw1 Et6/2/1 optic and replace it, then verify DMZ receive levels, link state at both ends and error counters. Use the combined readings to reach this diagnosis; Remote Fault alone is not a universal failed-optic indicator.
questions.commandHint: Compare spine MAC detail with DMZ transceiver readings: Remote Fault True on spine and -30.00 dBm Rx on DMZ point back to the spine optic. Which component should you replace?

questions.prompt: Does the spine PHY State linkUp mean this interface is operational?

options.text: No. Spine Interface State is linkDown, status is notconnect and Remote Fault remains True.
options.feedback: Read PHY and interface state separately.

options.text: Yes. PHY State overrides Interface State and the status output.
options.feedback: The captured Interface State and status both show the member down.

options.text: Yes. The different Po302 and Po321 numbers prove a healthy aggregate.
options.feedback: Local port-channel numbers do not establish member or service health.

questions.explanation: The spine PHY is up while its interface is down. The DMZ PHY and interface are both down. Preserve these distinct states; do not replace them with a single generic linkUp. The port-channel membership shown in status is context, not evidence of a bundle configuration fault.
questions.commandHint: Request status and MAC detail on the spine, then compare the same commands on the DMZ.

questions.prompt: What do the zero error counters tell you?

options.text: The link carried error-free traffic between both captures.
options.feedback: Traffic is not established by these counters, and both interfaces are down.

options.text: There is no optical fault because FCS and Symbol are zero.
options.feedback: A down link can have zero frame-error counters despite an optical fault.

options.text: We do not see actively incrementing errors on either port; the counters remain zero in both captures.
options.feedback: Correct. No increase is visible in the supplied error-counter readings.

questions.explanation: All displayed error counters remain zero in both captures, so we do not see errors actively incrementing in these readings. The link is still down: zero errors do not establish that traffic is passing or that the optic is healthy. Continue to use status, MAC faults and transceiver readings to diagnose the failure.
questions.commandHint: Select counters errors for each switch and compare the two readings shown together. Look for any counter that increases.

questions.prompt: What does comparing the two MAC snapshots show?

options.text: The link is repeatedly bouncing within the last minute.
options.feedback: The captured Changes totals do not increase between the supplied samples.

options.text: The same fault and interface states persist, with unchanged Changes totals over 41 seconds on spine and 39 seconds on DMZ.
options.feedback: Use each endpoint’s actual MAC timestamps and compare its own rows.

options.text: Both endpoints were measured over exactly the same 60-second interval.
options.feedback: The timestamps show different intervals, neither of them 60 seconds.

questions.explanation: Spine MAC time advances from 23:59:30 to 00:00:11 (41 seconds); DMZ advances from 23:59:35 to 00:00:14 (39 seconds), across midnight. All displayed state/fault Changes totals stay unchanged within each pair. These captures show a persistent fault, not newly recorded bouncing during those intervals. They do not establish longer-term stability or the timing of the separate optics/error captures.
questions.commandHint: Select MAC detail, then Follow-up capture, for each switch. Compare Current System Time, Current State and Changes row by row.

outcome.title: Spine optic replacement restored the link
outcome.summary: The operator confirmed that replacing the spine-gw1 Et6/2/1 optic fixed the link to dmz-gw2 Et6/21/1.
outcome.limits: Post-repair optical readings, error counters and a measured stability interval were not supplied. Whether fibers were also cleaned or reseated was not specified; do not claim those actions occurred or that they were excluded.

captureNeeds: Add the actual post-repair readings if available, and clarify whether any fiber cleaning or reseating accompanied the confirmed spine optic replacement. Link recovery is already confirmed.
Collect the same four interface-specific commands at both endpoints after repair, then repeat them over a stated monitoring interval. Preserve timestamps and reset/intervention history.
If retained, provide actual capture timestamps for the repeated counters/transceiver outputs. Their Last Update ages are not capture timestamps.

The operator confirmed spine optic replacement fixed the problem; numerical post-repair readings and a measured stability interval were not supplied. The spine line card was not specified for this incident.

questions.prompt: Which optic has failed, and what should you replace?

options.text: Replace the leaf-gw2 Et55/1 optic solely because that port records the receive errors.
options.feedback: The receiving port records the symptoms. Follow its low receive signal back toward the spine transmitter and compare both fault histories.

options.text: Replace the spine-gw1 Et4/28/1 optic. Leaf errors and low lane 4 Rx agree with increasing spine Remote Fault and leaf Local Fault counts.
options.feedback: Correct. These combined observations point to the spine optic as the failed component to replace in this case.

options.text: Replace neither optic because both ports currently show connected.
options.feedback: A connected link can still suffer optical errors and intermittent faults.

questions.explanation: Leaf lane 4 Rx is -14.91 dBm in both readings while its receive errors increase. Leaf Local Fault Changes rise from 1088 to 1096; spine Remote Fault Changes rise from 1058 to 1066. Together they support the spine-to-leaf fault direction and replacement of the spine optic. Verify receive power, new errors and stability after replacement; a Remote Fault count alone does not identify a failed component.
questions.commandHint: Compare leaf transceiver and counters errors with MAC detail at both ends. Follow the affected receive direction back to the transmitting optic.

questions.prompt: Does connected / linkUp mean this link is healthy?

options.text: No. Both ports are up in the snapshots, but leaf errors and MAC state/fault changes increase between readings.
options.feedback: Correct. Current state and recent stability are different observations.

options.text: Yes. Connected status means the optical signal and traffic must be healthy.
options.feedback: Connected describes the current state; it does not cancel the increasing errors or state changes.

options.text: Yes. Local Fault and Remote Fault are False now, so there have been no recent faults.
options.feedback: False is the sampled fault state. The increasing Changes counters show recent fault activity.

questions.explanation: Both status outputs say connected and both MAC snapshots show linkUp. Nevertheless, interface-state Changes increase by four at each end. The leaf PHY Changes also rise by four, while the spine PHY Changes stay at four. Read each row separately: the link can be up at capture time and still be unstable.
questions.commandHint: Compare the status result with both MAC snapshots. Check Changes even when Current State is linkUp or False.

questions.prompt: What do the repeated error counters show?

options.text: Only old errors; no counter increases between the leaf readings.
options.feedback: The later leaf reading is higher in four categories, so these are not just unchanged historical totals.

options.text: Exactly 18 FCS errors per second on the leaf.
options.feedback: FCS increases by 18, but the error-command capture interval was not supplied; this is not a per-second rate.

options.text: Errors are incrementing on leaf-gw2: FCS 4 → 22, Symbol 4 → 22, Rx 6 → 26 and Runts 2 → 4. Spine counters remain zero.
options.feedback: Correct. The repeated readings show increasing receive-side errors on the leaf.

questions.explanation: Leaf FCS and Symbol each increase by 18, Rx by 20 and Runts by 2. Align, Giants and Tx stay zero; all displayed spine counters stay zero. Keep the categories separate rather than adding overlapping counters into a unique-error total. The supplied readings and operator report establish increasing errors; no timed error rate is available.
questions.commandHint: Select counters errors for each endpoint. Compare each column between the two displayed readings.

questions.prompt: What do the increasing fault counts in show interfaces ethernet XX mac detail on each device tell you?

options.text: There are no faults because the current Local Fault and Remote Fault values are False.
options.feedback: The flags are False at capture time, but their increasing Changes totals record activity between captures.

options.text: Leaf Local Fault and spine Remote Fault Changes each increase by 8, supporting a recurring spine-to-leaf receive problem.
options.feedback: Correct. The paired histories support the same direction as the leaf receive-power and error readings.

options.text: The counters prove exactly eight complete link down/up cycles at both ends.
options.feedback: Fault-state changes are not complete link cycles. Read the separate interface-state Changes rows.

questions.explanation: Leaf Local Fault Changes rise 1088 → 1096 over 93 seconds; spine Remote Fault Changes rise 1058 → 1066 over 85 seconds. Leaf Remote Fault stays at 6 and spine Local Fault stays at 8. This pattern supports the affected spine-to-leaf direction. The sampling windows differ, so matching deltas are corroborating evidence, not proof of eight simultaneous events or eight complete flaps.
questions.commandHint: Select MAC detail at each endpoint. Compare the two Local/Remote Fault Changes columns and their Current System Time values.

outcome.title: Spine optic replacement fixed the problem
outcome.summary: The operator confirmed that the technician replaced the spine-gw1 Et4/28/1 optic and fixed the problem on the link to leaf-gw2 Et55/1.
outcome.limits: Numerical post-repair receive levels, error counters and a measured stability interval were not supplied. Any accompanying fiber cleaning or reseating was not specified.

captureNeeds: Collect the same four commands at both endpoints after the confirmed spine optic replacement, then repeat over a stated monitoring interval.
If retained, provide the error/transceiver capture timestamps, timezone and reset history. MAC timestamps apply only to the MAC samples.
Record whether any fiber cleaning or reseating accompanied the replacement; provide the spine line-card inventory if available.

cases.title: The persistent down link
cases.intro: A 100G link is down between spine-gw1 Et8/10/1 and leaf-gw2 Et53/1. Compare both endpoints and decide how to sequence the repair and follow-up checks.
cases.method: Read the Bias Current (mA) column and subtract the lowest of the four lane values from the highest to find the bias current variance between lanes. Compare that range with the operator’s usual 10–20 mA maximum spread. Follow each transmitter toward the opposite receiver and correlate paired fault flags to sequence the repair.
cases.limits: Timezone, line cards and counter reset history were not supplied. All post-repair recordings are missing. No completed replacement or recovery was reported. The usual 10–20 mA maximum bias current variance between lanes is operator guidance for this environment, not a universal manufacturer alarm threshold.
cases.collectionNote: Fourteen supplied interface recordings: status once per endpoint; optics, MAC and error counters twice per endpoint. The two leaf error tables were supplied in an owner follow-up; their capture times are unknown. MAC timestamps span 45 seconds on spine and 105 seconds on leaf. Leaf Last Change ages advance by 104 seconds; preserve that discrepancy. Optical Last Update values are telemetry ages, not capture intervals.

options.text: Replace spine-gw1 Et8/10/1 first because the bias current variance between its four lanes is about 36 mA.
options.feedback: The high bias current variance between lanes on spine-gw1 needs follow-up after the leaf optic replacement; it does not make the spine optic the first replacement target.

options.text: Replace leaf-gw2 Et53/1 first, using the low spine Rx and paired fault flags to follow the affected direction.
options.feedback: Yes. The combined evidence and the supplied runbook prioritize the leaf optic.

options.text: Replace both optics at once before collecting any follow-up readings.
options.feedback: Separate the interventions: replace the leaf optic first and assess the result before considering the spine optic.

questions.explanation: Spine lane 1 Rx is -13.87 dBm in both samples with Local Fault True. Leaf Remote Fault is True and lane 1 Tx is -5.36 dBm. The affected direction is leaf Tx toward spine Rx. The owner recommends replacing the leaf optic first. Remote Fault alone is not a universal failed-optic indicator; the recommendation is not a reported repair result.
questions.commandHint: Open transceiver and mac detail on both switches. Follow leaf Tx toward spine Rx and compare Local/Remote Fault. Reassess the high bias current variance between lanes on spine-gw1 after replacing the leaf optic.

questions.prompt: What does the bias current variance between lanes on spine-gw1 tell you?

options.text: About 36 mA of bias current variance between lanes is unusually high; reassess it after replacing the leaf optic first.
options.feedback: Yes. The highest and lowest lanes are about 36 mA apart, well beyond the operator’s usual 10–20 mA maximum spread.

options.text: The bias current on one lane changed by 36 mA over time, so replace the spine-gw1 optic first.
options.feedback: The 36 mA is the difference between the highest and lowest lane readings in one capture. Each individual lane changes very little between captures.

options.text: Proof that the spine optic is healthy because every lane has nonzero bias current.
options.feedback: Nonzero current does not establish health. Compare the highest and lowest readings: their approximately 36 mA difference is unusually large for this environment.

questions.explanation: Read the Bias Current (mA) column on spine-gw1: 63.35, 44.00, 39.24 and 27.33 mA. Highest minus lowest is 63.35 − 27.33 = 36.02 mA. In the next capture, 63.39 − 27.30 = 36.09 mA. These ranges of 36.02 and 36.09 mA are the bias current variance between lanes meant in this lesson. The operator normally sees at most about 10–20 mA between the four lanes, so roughly 36 mA is a very large spread. Replace leaf-gw2 first. Consider the spine-gw1 optic only if the link remains down and this high variance persists after the leaf swap.
questions.commandHint: Open the spine-gw1 transceiver readings. In the Bias Current (mA) column, find the highest and lowest of the four lanes: 63.35 and 27.33. Subtract to get 36.02 mA. Compare with the operator’s usual 10–20 mA maximum spread, then repeat for the second capture.

questions.prompt: What can the repeated MAC and error captures establish?

options.text: The link is healthy because both endpoints show zero error counters in both samples.
options.feedback: Both status and MAC captures show a down link. Zero errors on that link do not establish health or service.

options.text: The accumulated MAC Changes prove the link is actively flapping during these samples.
options.feedback: The Changes totals do not increase between samples. Historical totals alone do not show new flaps in these windows.

options.text: Both ends remain down with unchanged MAC Changes, and all error counters stay zero in both samples at each endpoint.
options.feedback: Yes. Both endpoints remain down without new recorded MAC transitions or increasing error counters. Zero errors do not make this down link healthy.

questions.explanation: Spine MAC snapshots span 45 seconds and leaf snapshots span 105 seconds. Their state/fault Changes totals remain unchanged and both interfaces stay linkDown. Both error-counter samples at each endpoint show zero FCS, Align, Symbol, Rx, Runts, Giants and Tx. The counter captures have no absolute timestamps or reset baseline, so do not infer a measured error rate or recovery.
questions.commandHint: Compare both mac detail timestamps and Changes columns, then compare the two counters errors tables at each endpoint. All seven error categories remain zero; read that alongside the down link state.

questions.prompt: After replacing the leaf-gw2 optic, when could you consider replacing the spine-gw1 optic?

options.text: Whenever the bias current variance between lanes on spine-gw1 stays high, even if the link has recovered.
options.feedback: High bias current variance between lanes alone is insufficient here. The link must also remain down after the leaf optic replacement.

options.text: Only if the link remains down AND the bias current variance between lanes on spine-gw1 stays high after the leaf swap.
options.feedback: Yes. Recheck both conditions after replacing leaf-gw2 Et53/1: a still-down link and persistently high bias current variance between the four lanes. Only then consider replacing spine-gw1 Et8/10/1.

options.text: Whenever the link remains down after the leaf swap, even if the bias current variance between lanes has returned to normal.
options.feedback: A down link alone is insufficient for this second replacement. The high bias current variance between lanes on spine-gw1 must also persist; otherwise continue investigating.

Neither condition alone is sufficient. Record each intervention separately and verify optics, fault states, new errors, stability and service. No swap or recovery has been reported.

captureNeeds: After replacing leaf-gw2 Et53/1, capture both-end status, transceiver, mac detail and timed error counters with reset history. Calculate bias current variance between lanes on spine-gw1: highest minus lowest in the Bias Current (mA) column.

Only if both continued link failure and high bias current variance between lanes on spine-gw1 persist after the leaf swap, consider replacing spine-gw1 Et8/10/1 and repeat both-end verification. Compare the measured range with the operator’s usual 10–20 mA maximum spread. Record each intervention and outcome separately.
